summary: UN climate talks end with no overall deal, the deepest explosive volcanic deposits turn up beside the Challenger Deep, and papers on ocean nitrogen, chips that report from inside reactions, and a weighed black hole in the early universe.

news.title: COP31 ends without an overall agreement after the EU and island states reject a text that does not name fossil fuels
news.tldr: The UN climate summit in Antalya closed on Sunday with its main political text unadopted, the first such outcome since 2000, after a dispute over whether to mention fossil fuels.
news.why_selected: A rare collapse of the UN climate process's headline decision, with direct consequences for how climate science feeds into the 2028 global stocktake.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: The annual UN climate conference, known as a COP, takes its decisions by consensus, so any one of the nearly 200 participating countries can block a text. Each summit usually ends with a "cover decision", an overarching political document that records what was agreed and signals the direction of future action. COP31 was held in Antalya, Turkey, with Turkey presiding and Australia leading the negotiations. In 2023, at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: The proposed cover decision, called the Antalya Pact, was not adopted. According to Health Policy Watch, a first draft released on 16 November called for an immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems, but that language was removed after objections from oil-producing states. The final proposal, issued early on Sunday, did not mention coal, oil or gas and referred only obliquely to the 2023 agreement. The European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Norway and several small island states rejected it, while a Saudi-led group and Russia said they could not accept any wording on fossil fuels. COP31 President Murat Kurum told the closing session there was no agreement and that the decisions had not been adopted. The talks ran 44 hours past their scheduled close, making this the longest UN climate conference on record.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: It is the first summit since COP6 in The Hague in 2000 to end with no high-level decision document. The failed draft would have set a goal of raising electricity's share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 and expressed "deep concern" that warming would cross the 1.5C limit set in the Paris Agreement. Countries also clashed over an attempt by Saudi Arabia, India and Kenya to delay the next reports of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which many governments want published before a 2028 stocktake of emission-cutting efforts.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: Unresolved items carry over automatically to COP32 in Addis Ababa in November 2027. Australia's negotiations chief pointed to a separate commitment on faster electrification signed by more than 90 countries.

news.title: Robot dives beside the Challenger Deep recover the deepest explosive volcanic deposits ever documented
news.tldr: Seven remotely operated dives on the Mariana Trench wall found rocks from explosive eruptions at more than 6,000 metres depth, in a zone where young volcanism is not expected.
news.why_selected: A peer-reviewed field result that extends the known depth limit of explosive volcanism and bears on why the ocean's deepest point is so deep.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: The Mariana Trench marks where the Pacific plate sinks beneath the Philippine Sea plate, a process called subduction. Its deepest part, the Challenger Deep, lies almost 11,000 metres below sea level. The strip of the overriding plate between a trench and its volcanoes is called the forearc. Forearcs are generally considered poor places to find young lava, because the mantle beneath them is usually not hot enough to melt. Explosive eruptions are also thought to be muted in deep water, since high pressure keeps the gas dissolved in magma from expanding.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.body: A team led by Robert Stern of the University of Texas at Dallas reports in Frontiers in Earth Science on a late-2024 cruise that used the remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which can dive to 6,500 metres. It made seven dives across roughly 300 kilometres of a 550-kilometre forearc segment next to the Challenger Deep. In the western part the team recovered pyroclastic rocks, meaning rocks built from fragments thrown out by explosive eruptions, from deeper than 6,000 metres. The paper calls them the deepest known pyroclastic deposits and suggests the eruptions were driven by supercritical fluids and were less explosive than their low-pressure equivalents. The eastern part instead exposes older mantle rock.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The contrast suggests the forearc is being stretched east to west in two ways: by mechanical pulling in the east and by the addition of fresh magma in the west. The authors estimate the segment is stretching at about 45 millimetres a year or more. The work also supports an explanation for the trench's depth: the two plates are weakly attached, and the sinking plate is narrow and short, so it bends steeply.

sections.heading: What to watch
sections.body: The eruption sites have not been located, and Stern says the hot flows probably did not travel far, because they kept enough heat to weld into hard rock. The team says more sampling and radiometric dating are needed to test the two-style stretching idea. The seafloor between 6,500 and 11,000 metres remains unsampled by this group, whose vehicle cannot go deeper.

papers.title: Atmospheric organic nitrogen is a major nutrient source to global oceans
affiliations: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; Southern University of Science and Technology; Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology; East China Normal University; Ocean University of China; South China University of Technology
papers.tldr: Measurements from 21 research cruises and a global chemistry model put atmospheric organic nitrogen falling on the oceans at 12.8 million tonnes a year, about 27% of all nitrogen deposition.
papers.why_selected: Puts a number on a long-neglected part of the global nitrogen cycle, using the broadest open-ocean dataset so far; top of the shortlist by venue and coverage.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Nitrogen is a nutrient that limits the growth of marine life across large parts of the ocean. Some of it arrives from the air on tiny particles called aerosols, in two broad forms: inorganic, such as nitrate and ammonium, and organic, meaning nitrogen bound into carbon-containing molecules. How much the organic part contributes has been unclear.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Organic nitrogen has usually been measured indirectly, by determining total nitrogen and subtracting the inorganic part. According to the authors' institution, this subtraction is laborious and error-prone, and it has left major gaps in global datasets.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: The team had previously developed a high-sensitivity method that measures organic and inorganic nitrogen in an aerosol sample at the same time, removing the need for subtraction. Here they applied it to 418 marine aerosol samples collected on 21 research cruises, from tropical waters to the Arctic and Southern oceans. They then used those observations to constrain a three-dimensional model of atmospheric chemistry, which simulates where organic nitrogen is emitted, how it is transformed in the air and where it lands. The ship measurements act as checkpoints; the model fills in the rest of the globe.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: Aerosol organic nitrogen varied by more than three orders of magnitude, lowest over the remote Southern Ocean and highest over the Yellow Sea, and averaged 30% of total aerosol nitrogen. The model gives 12.8 million tonnes deposited to the oceans each year, about 27% of total nitrogen deposition, and around half in nitrogen-limited regions such as the central Atlantic and the Indonesian seas. The largest sources are biomass burning (4.8 million tonnes), marine aerosol emissions (3.9 million) and imines formed chemically in the atmosphere (2.2 million). Non-marine sources supply 8.9 million tonnes, 70% of the total.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: If roughly a quarter of airborne nitrogen input has been under-counted, estimates of ocean productivity need revisiting, and changes in wildfires and human emissions could shift nutrient supply far offshore. The caveat is that the global total comes from a model constrained by ship samples, not from direct measurement of deposition everywhere.

papers.title: Telemetric calorimetry for wireless continuous reaction profiling
affiliations: Stanford University; Cornell University; Emory University; OWiC Technologies
papers.tldr: Chips smaller than a grain of rice sit inside test tubes and wirelessly report the temperature of a chemical reaction every half-second.
papers.why_selected: A new measurement capability for routine chemistry, turning one end-point result per reaction into a continuous record across whole batches.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Chemists who search for new reactions often run them in batches of 96 small tubes. A sample from every finished tube has to go through a separate instrument, which can take minutes to hours per sample, so a batch may take a couple of days to process and yields one data point per reaction.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: According to the Stanford account of the work, the alternatives to waiting for the end were to withdraw samples during the reaction, which disturbs it, or to use customised, expensive monitoring instruments.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: Nearly every chemical reaction gives off or absorbs heat, so the temperature of the mixture over time traces how the reaction is progressing. Measuring heat flow is called calorimetry. The team adapted microelectronic chips known as Optical Wireless Integrated Circuits so that they survive inside a reaction mixture: each is a very small piece of silicon semiconductor covered with a chemically resistant material. Placed in a tube, a chip senses temperature and wirelessly transmits it to a computer throughout the reaction. Lead researcher Song Lin compares it to giving each reaction its own cell phone, so that it can report how it is doing.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: Each chip relays a data point every half-second. For a 96-tube batch and an hour-long reaction that is 7,200 points per tube, or nearly 700,000 in total, against 96 from end-point analysis. In one test, a potential catalyst poison, a substance that stops a catalyst from working, was added to each tube; the traces showed whether the reaction shut down and often why. In another, small-scale runs revealed when a reaction released too much heat, a safety concern, and how conditions could be adjusted to reduce it.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: Dense, cheap, non-intrusive data could speed up reaction discovery for drugs and materials, and the researchers envision chips that sense conductivity, light transmission or acidity. A caveat: several authors are founders of, or advisers to, the company that makes the chips, as the competing-interests statement discloses.

papers.title: Resolving the black hole sphere of influence in a hyperluminous obscured quasar at redshift 4.6
papers.tldr: Radio observations of gas swirling at the centre of the most luminous known obscured quasar give the first motion-based mass for a supermassive black hole beyond redshift 2.
papers.why_selected: A first direct weighing of a black hole in the early universe, which tests the indirect mass estimates that studies of early black hole growth rely on.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Supermassive black holes sit at the centres of galaxies, and their masses are central to understanding how the two grow together. The most direct way to weigh one is to watch gas or stars moving inside its sphere of influence, the region where the black hole's gravity dominates over the galaxy's. In the early universe such measurements have been missing.

sections.heading: Existing approaches
sections.body: Masses of distant, actively feeding black holes, called quasars, are normally estimated from a single spectrum, using the width of emission lines and an empirical relation. Whether that "single-epoch" method holds for the most luminous distant quasars has been questioned. Earlier ALMA attempts on quasars at redshift above 6 found no unambiguous signal.

sections.heading: Key idea
sections.body: The authors reasoned that those attempts may have failed because intense radiation near an exposed quasar strips carbon of the electrons needed to produce the far-infrared emission line of ionised carbon, written [C II], that ALMA observes. A quasar buried in dust should shield that gas. They therefore targeted W2246-0526, the most luminous obscured quasar known, seen at redshift 4.6, when the universe was about 1.3 billion years old. After separating out gas flowing outward, they measured the spread of gas velocities in a series of rings around the centre. If a large mass sits in the middle, gas closer in must move faster.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body: In the preprint version of the paper, which is the version read for this summary, the velocity spread rises toward the centre inside about 0.78 kiloparsecs and is flat farther out. Fitting a black hole plus the host galaxy gives a mass of 6.3 billion Suns, with a quoted uncertainty of 0.14 billion, and a sphere of influence about 2.3 kiloparsecs across. That agrees, within errors, with the earlier single-epoch estimate of about 4 billion.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The agreement suggests that spectrum-based masses may be reliable for such extreme objects, and that dust-obscured quasars are good targets for more direct measurements. The caveat: this is one exceptional object in a turbulent, merging system, and the result depends on modelling its outflows.
